title: A security page that a buyer can finish
metaTitle: A security page buyers can finish
excerpt: A security page should say where data lives, who can see it, and how to ask a harder question. A pasted policy does not answer those three, and most buyers will not read it.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, a security page sketched as answers a buyer can finish.
caption: A stylus over wireframes. A security page is a set of answers, not a policy paste. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What three questions should a startup security page answer?
faqs.answer: Where the data lives, who can see it, and how to ask something harder. Name the kind of data you hold and the place it is stored, in words a non-lawyer can read. Link the policy. Do not make the policy the only answer.

faqs.question: Should you put a certification badge on the page before you have it?
faqs.answer: No. A badge you have earned can sit beside the answers, with its scope and date. A badge you hope to earn is a roadmap item. In progress next to a certification is a promise procurement will cite if the date slips.

faqs.question: How should a buyer ask a question the page does not answer?
faqs.answer: Give one path a person will actually read, and say what to include, such as the company name and whether a questionnaire is attached. Say what you will not finish the same day. A locked portal with no public answers makes reviewers assume the answers are missing.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A security page a buyer can finish answers three questions. Where does the data live. Who can see it. How do I ask something harder. A startup security page that pastes a policy, a badge, or a wall of product names has not answered them. The buyer still has to write to you, and they will, with less patience.

Write the three answers in the first screen, in sentences. The policy can sit behind them. It cannot stand in for them.

## Where the data lives

Name the kind of data you actually hold. Account names, messages, files, payment details, health notes, children's information, whatever is true. Then say where it is stored, in language a non-lawyer can read. A region. A known class of provider. Whether you keep it in one place or copy it to a second one for backup.

If you do not know, the page is not ready. "Industry-standard cloud" is a way of saying you have not looked. Look, and write the fact you are willing to repeat on a call. If the fact is "we are moving regions this quarter," say that, with the date you mean. A page that hides a migration will be contradicted by the first security questionnaire.

Separate your systems from your customers' systems. A marketing site on a host is not the same statement as a product database. Buyers conflate them when you do. One short heading for the product, one line for the site, if both matter. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration, is a reminder that a shop holds orders and customer details. Thomas Bewick, a heritage editorial site, holds a different kind of record. The page should match the product you actually operate, not a generic SaaS diagram.

Say how long you keep it, if you know. If retention depends on the customer's settings, say who controls the setting. "We keep data forever unless you ask" and "you can export and delete from the admin" are different products. Write the one you ship.

Payments are their own sentence. If a processor handles card numbers and you do not store them, say that plainly. If you do store something sensitive, do not imply that you do not. Google's helpful-content guidance treats trust as the center of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, and it gives extra weight to topics that affect money, safety, or welfare. A security page is that kind of page. A vague sentence is not a neutral design choice. It is a trust choice.

## Who can see it

Say who, inside your company, can open customer data, and why. Support, on a request. Engineering, when a bug requires it. Nobody, as a hobby. You do not need a surveillance essay. You need the rule a buyer can repeat to their own security person.

Say who, on the customer's side, can see it. Admins, every user, a private workspace. If a setting changes that, name the setting. "Permissions follow the roles you create" is a useful sentence only if the product actually has roles. If it does not, do not borrow the sentence from a company that does.

Say whether you share data with subprocessors that do a job: email delivery, error logs, file storage, analytics. List the jobs, not a logo wall of every tool you have ever tried. A name and a job. "Error logs go to a logging service. They can include account identifiers. They should not include the contents of a message." If you are not sure they do not, fix the product before you write the softer line.

Say what you do not do. You do not sell the data. You do not use customer content to train a model, if that is true. If you do, say so, and say what opt-out exists. A hidden practice is the thing a buyer will feel lied to about later, even if a clause in the policy mentioned it. The page is where you put the fact a person will actually read.

Access for Hanabi's own client work is a different question from a multi-tenant product. On a client project, the client owns the accounts, and the portal holds brand files, docs, and updates. That is not a security white paper. It is an ownership fact. Your page should be just as concrete about your product, at the level you can defend.

## How to ask a harder question

Every buyer with a real risk will have a fourth question. A questionnaire. A data processing agreement. A penetration test summary. A question about a specific field you store. The page should tell them how to ask, and what they will get.

Give one path. An email address a person reads, or a form that creates a ticket your team expects. Say what to include: the company name, the question, and whether a questionnaire is attached. Say what you will not do on a first reply. You may not complete a forty-page spreadsheet the same day. You can acknowledge it and name a time you will keep.

If you have a document you can hand over, link it. A current policy, a list of subprocessors, a one-page summary of the three answers. Date the document. An undated PDF is how last year's architecture stays in circulation. If you do not have a document, the three answers on the page are still better than a badge.

Do not make the harder question a scavenger hunt through a trust portal with six locked rooms and a login. A portal can be useful once the buyer is serious. The public page should let them know the door exists. If the only next step is "contact sales," a security reviewer will assume you are hiding the absence of an answer. Give the reviewer a path that does not require them to pretend they are buying today.

Write the path in the same voice as the rest of the site. A sudden shift into legalese tells the reader the careful sentences above were marketing. Keep the lawyer's document available. Keep the page in the language of the product.

## What not to paste in place of the answers

Do not paste the full privacy policy into the hero. People will not read it there. Nielsen Norman Group's work on page time is the practical reason: visitors often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text even when they stay. The three answers have to fit that window. The policy remains the policy, linked and titled as a policy.

Do not paste a framework's logo because a competitor has it. A badge you have earned can sit beside the answers, with the scope and the date. A badge you intend to pursue is a roadmap item, not a mark on the page. "In progress" next to a certification is a promise. If the date slips, the page is what procurement will cite.

Do not list security features you have not shipped. Encryption in transit is ordinary and worth a sentence if it is true. "Military-grade," "bank-level," and "unhackable" are not facts. They are the sentences a careful buyer uses to disqualify you. Use the plain version. What you encrypt. What you do not store. How a customer revokes access.

Do not hide the page. Link it from the footer and from the pricing or security-related question on the sales page. A startup that makes the buyer search for the word security has already answered, poorly.

## Keeping the page true

Name an owner. When the architecture changes, the sentences change in the same week. A stale security page is worse than a short one, because it creates a contradiction you will have to explain under pressure.

Review it when you add a subprocessor, a new kind of data, or a new region. The review is a diff of facts, not a redesign. The layout can stay boring. Boring is a feature on this page. Buyers are looking for something they can finish, not for a brand film.

Read it once a year against the product, with someone who did not write it. Ask them to point at each sentence and say where in the product or the contract it is true. Any sentence they cannot place gets rewritten or removed. This is the same discipline as design QA. The real system is the subject. The page is the claim.

Store the supporting docs next to the brand files, wherever your team will find the current version. A Hanabi client portal is one model: docs and updates in a known place after delivery. Your equivalent might be the repo, the drive, or the trust center. Pick one. Two copies will diverge.

The page should still look like your site. Same type. Same width. Readable on a phone, because the reviewer is often reading between meetings. The WCAG principles, perceivable and understandable, matter here as much as on the product. A security page set in low-contrast display type fails the people you are trying to reassure.

## The rest of the truth, nearby

Security questions often arrive with a list of tools. The buyer wants to know what connects, not only where the data sits. Those are related and not the same page. A security page that becomes an integrations catalog will do both jobs badly.

Answer the three questions here. Then, if they need the catalog, send them to a page that lists what actually connects, what the connection does, and what it does not. The piece on [integrations pages that tell the truth](/blog/integrations-pages-that-tell-the-truth) is the next read when the questionnaire moves from storage to "does it talk to our warehouse."

If you want to see how a studio presents work without padding it with claims it cannot support, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The same restraint belongs on a security page. Facts a buyer can finish. A path for the harder question. Nothing you would have to walk back.
